You pass on what someone else said (reported speech): dice que…, me dijo que…, me preguntó si…
the message (passed on by someone else)
He told me he was tired.
He asked me if I wanted to go.
To pass on what someone says now: dice que + present.
To pass on what someone said in the past: dijo que + imperfect / pluscuamperfecto / conditional.
To pass on questions: me preguntó si…, me preguntó dónde…
To change pronouns and time expressions correctly (yo → él, hoy → ese día).
To tell a big piece of news you heard from someone else.
Lucía calls Ana, very excited. Javier told her something important last night. Then Ana passes the news on to Mihai.
Ana! You won’t believe it! Last night Javier proposed to me.
Whaaat?! Tell me everything! What exactly did he say?
He told me he loved me very much and that I was the woman of his life.
Then he asked me if I wanted to marry him. And he took out a gorgeous ring!
I told him yes, of course! And he explained that he had been planning everything for months.
How romantic! Do Mum and Dad know?
Not yet. Javier says he wants to tell them himself on Sunday, over lunch.
(Later, with Mihai) Mihai, I’ve got news, but it’s a secret until Sunday.
I promise not to say anything. What’s happened?
Lucía told me that Javier proposed to her last night. They’re getting married!
That’s great! Yesterday Javier asked me if I knew a good jeweller’s… Now I understand!
And Lucía says she wants a small wedding… but knowing Mum, it’ll be huge.
Ha, ha. Listen… would you like a big wedding or a small one?
Are you asking me seriously, Mihai Popescu?
“no te lo vas a creer” = you won’t believe it
“me pidió la mano” = he proposed to me
“se van a casar” = they’re going to get married
In reported speech, “que” is unstressed: “dice que viene” = “diceke BYEH-neh”. A surprised “¿Qué?” is stressed!
Stress on the first syllable, even with two pronouns attached: CUÉN-ta-me-lo.
Spaniards lower and slow their voice when telling a secret: “Es un secreto…”, then rise for the big news: “¡Se van a casar!”.
1. Reported speech in the present: DICE QUE
When you pass on what someone says NOW (or always says), the verb tense does NOT change. You only change the pronouns:
Dice que quiere una boda pequeña.
Dice que ha visto a Javier.
Just like in English: “I’m happy” → “She says she’s happy”. Only the person changes (I → she).
2. Reported speech in the past: DIJO QUE
When the reporting verb is in the past (dijo, explicó, comentó), the tense in reported speech “takes a step back”:
«Te quiero» → Me dijo que me quería.
«Lo he preparado» → Dijo que lo había preparado.
Good news: English does the same! “He said he LOVED me” (not “loves”) → “Me dijo que me QUERÍA” (imperfect). Follow your English instinct and you’ll get it right.
If the information is still true, Spaniards sometimes keep the present: “Me dijo que es de Valencia”. But the general rule is the step back.
For yes / no questions → SI (if). For questions with a question word → keep the word (with its accent):
Me preguntó si quería casarme con él.
Me preguntó si conocía una joyería.
Don’t put “que” before “si”: “Me preguntó si…”, not “me preguntó que si…” (although many Spaniards do it in relaxed speech).
4. What else changes: pronouns, time, place
He said he would come there the next day.
For requests (“he asked me to…”) Spanish uses the subjunctive: “Me pidió que fuera”. You’ll learn it at B1. Until then: “Me pidió ayuda” (he asked me for help).
After “dijo que”, the present becomes the imperfect.
He asked me if I wanted to go.
He explained that he had prepared everything.

How a piece of news changes as it passes from mouth to mouth. A little game of “Chinese whispers” in Ana’s family.
On Monday, Lucía told Ana that Javier had proposed to her.
Ana promised she wouldn’t say anything… but that evening she told Mihai.
On Tuesday, Mihai mentioned to Kenji that Lucía and Javier were going to get married in spring.
Kenji explained to Lena that the wedding would be in Valencia, on the beach.
On Wednesday, Lena told Tom that there would be five hundred guests and fireworks.
On Thursday, Tom asked Pablo if it was true that Lucía was pregnant.
Pablo, surprised, called his mother and asked her why nobody had told him anything.
His mother, Carmen, answered that she didn’t know what he was talking about.
On Sunday, at the family lunch, Javier stood up and said: “I have something to announce.”
“Lucía and I are getting married.” Everyone answered at the same time: “We already knew!”
Lucía looked at Ana. Ana looked at Mihai. And Grandma Rosario laughed louder than anyone.
“se iban a casar” = were going to get married
One rainy afternoon, Ana asked her grandmother: “Grandma, how did you know Grandpa was the man of your life?”. Rosario put down her coffee and thought for a while.
“I’m going to tell you something I’ve never told anyone,” she said. “On the night we met, at the village fiesta, we danced all night. Well, he tried to dance.”
“When the music ended, he walked me home. At the door, he told me he had never met a girl like me.”
“I laughed and told him that’s what all the boys said to all the girls.”
“Then he went very serious. He told me he wasn’t like the others. He explained that his father had died the year before and that he had to work in the fields to help his mother.”
“He told me he had no money, no car and no house of his own. But that if I gave him a chance, he would work all his life to make me happy.”
“And what did you answer?”, Ana asked, moved.
“I told him I would think about it. A girl couldn’t say yes straight away!” Grandma laughed. “But that night I didn’t sleep a wink.”
“The next day my mother asked me why I was so distracted. I told her what Antonio had said to me. She looked at me and asked if he made me laugh.”
“I told her yes, a lot. And then she told me something I’ve never forgotten: that money is earned and lost, but a man who makes you laugh is a treasure.”
“A week later I said yes to Antonio. And my mother was right. Fifty years together and he never stopped making me laugh. Not even at the end, in hospital.”
“On his last day he told me he was leaving in peace, because he had kept the promise he made that night.”
Ana had tears in her eyes. Her grandmother took her hand.
“And now I’m asking you, the way my mother asked me: does Mihai make you laugh?”
Ana smiled through her tears. “Every day, Grandma. Especially when he tries to dance.”
That evening, when she got home, Ana told Mihai what her grandmother had told her. He listened in silence and then asked her if she wanted to dance.
They put an old song on the phone and danced in the kitchen. Mihai danced terribly, as usual. And Ana laughed, as usual.
Trabajar toda su vida para hacerla feliz
¿Qué le preguntó la madre de Rosario?
¿Cuándo hace reír Mihai a Ana sobre todo?
